action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment is non-negotiable. The pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference and must be characterized first under controlled conditions. Twelve trials will give adequate precision for a baseline mean and allow me to assess short-term stability on day one itself.

state.question: Why do all four instrument streams show near-zero or weakly negative cross-correlations at various time offsets, with individual 'echoes' of past readings also near chance level, despite having sufficient data density and trial counts to detect real structure if it existed?

hypotheses.label: Instruments are measuring independent noise processes with no shared physical signal
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-correlations (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: 0.242; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab: -0.328; etc.) are all substantially weaker than their respective chance levels would permit for systematic error. Even the 'best' cross-check (pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs at 0.345) barely exceeds a ±0.529 chance threshold at only n=30. If instruments were tracking a real common signal (e.g., thermal drift, gravitational anomaly, timing shifts), I would expect correlations well above chance even at various offsets. The absence of any consistently strong correlation—positive or negative—suggests each instrument is dominated by uncorrelated measurement noise. This is the mundane explanation: our instruments are not yet stable or sensitive enough to detect coherent variation, or there is no coherent variation to detect.

hypotheses.label: Instruments have inadequate temporal resolution or calibration drift is masking signal
hypotheses.rationale: All four streams show minimum value spacing of 0.000100, which is suspiciously uniform and round. This could indicate either (a) quantization/rounding in the readout electronics set to a fixed precision, or (b) genuine natural scatter. If quantization is present, it would artificially reduce apparent correlation by introducing systematic noise floor.
